muc.title: You saw the face and still got fooled
muc.text: A close friend messages asking to borrow money. Mark is careful and video calls, sees his friend's face for a few seconds, then the connection drops. Mark feels safe and sends the money. But the account was hacked, and that face was a deepfake.

muc.title: A fake face during the call
muc.text: Deepfakes can now run live during a call, putting someone else's face over the scammer's, as in video 14.

muc.title: Short, blurry, dropped
muc.text: Signs: the call is very short, the picture is blurry or choppy, then they blame a bad connection to hang up and switch to texting.

muc.title: Turn sideways, wave a hand across the face
muc.text: If you're suspicious, ask them to turn their face to the side, or wave a hand in front of their face. Fake faces often warp at those moments. But the technology keeps getting better, so don't rely on your eyes alone.

muc.title: Check through another channel
muc.text: The golden rule: check through another channel. Call the phone number you have saved, or ask a friend you both know.

muc.title: Report it right away
muc.text: If you already sent money, call your bank right away to ask them to stop the transaction, and report it to the police. The faster, the better your chances.

muc.title: Message your family group
muc.text: Message your family group: anyone asking to borrow money online, even on a video call, must be called back on their phone number to confirm.
